While quadrupeds have demonstrated versatility across various domains, their large-scale deployment remains limited, partly due to lack of application-specific designs. Roof environments represent a novel and unexplored use case, combining high safety risks for human workers with repetitive, strenuous tasks that could benefit from robotic assistance. A dedicated test rig of a roof's surface was designed to evaluate the baseline performance of a commercial quadruped, the \emph{Unitree Go2}, in this new environment. Experiments revealed that standard ball feet are inherently inadequate for locomotion on sloped roofs: slippage increased quadratically with incline angle, get-up and lie-down sequences were only possible on small inclines, and critical failures already occurred regularly on moderate inclines of 25°. Learn more × License: CC BY-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.12272v1 [cs.RO] 08 Oct 2026 Walking on Roofs: Exploring the Potential of Walking Robots for Construction Work on Roofs Bjoern-Felix Dettmar Arne Roennau E-mail: dettmar@kit.edu Abstract This paper investigates the feasibility of deploying quadruped walking robots for the automation of work in roof environments. While quadrupeds have demonstrated versatility across various domains, their large-scale deployment remains limited, partly due to lack of application-specific designs. Roof environments represent a novel and unexplored use case, combining high safety risks for human workers with repetitive, strenuous tasks that could benefit from robotic assistance. A dedicated test rig of a roof’s surface was designed to evaluate the baseline performance of a commercial quadruped, the Unitree Go2 , in this new environment. Experiments revealed that standard ball feet are inherently inadequate for locomotion on sloped roofs: slippage increased quadratically with incline angle, get-up and lie-down sequences were only possible on small inclines, and critical failures already occurred regularly on moderate inclines of 25 ° 25\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} . This work provides the first systematic assessment of quadruped locomotion in roof environments, highlighting both the potential and the current limitations of this application and establishes a baseline for future research. Effective solutions will require a combination of task-oriented foot designs, advanced contact mechanics and environment-specific control strategies, such as reinforcement learning for roof-adapted gaits. Keywords: walking robots, quadruped, roof environment, construction, locomotion, friction, stability, motion capture † † institute: Machine Intelligence and Robotics Lab at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), Germany Figure 1: Examples of the Unitree Go2 on the test rig while balancing (left), walking (middle) and overview of the test rig setup (right). 1 Introduction The construction industry is among the least automated sectors with respect to robotics, despite its substantial economic relevance Haghsheno et al. (2024) . Within this domain, work on roofs represents a particularly hazardous area. Tasks such as construction, maintenance, installation, and inspection expose workers to significant risks, with slipping and falling accidents constituting a major cause of fatalities Health and Safety Executive (2020) . At the same time, many tasks on roofs are physically demanding and repetitive, providing a strong motivation to explore robotic assistance. In Germany alone, the roofing industry employed over 99,000 workers across more than 13,500 companies in 2023, generating a sales volume of nearly 12.9 billion euros Zentralverband des Deutschen Dachdeckerhandwerks (2023) . This highlights both the scale of the sector and the potential impact of automation. Quadruped robots have become an increasingly active research field over the past decade and have consequently attracted growing interest from the industrial sector Majithia et al. (2024) . For commercial applications, both academia and industry have predominantly proposed sectors such as Inspection & Maintenance , Search & Rescue , and Military & Surveillance Li et al. (2025) . Although these tasks have been proposed for a long time and quadruped capabilities have rapidly advanced, commercialization and deployment in these applications remain limited. This is exemplified by Boston Dynamics , one of the earliest and best-known developers of quadrupedal robots, which reported deploying only about 2,100 units of their flagship model Spot in industrial settings by 2023 Boston Dynamics () . This is in strong contrast to the rapid development of quadrupedal capabilities. Today, quadrupeds exhibit high mobility, adaptability in complex environments, and increasing energy efficiency Li et al. (2025) ; Taheri and Mozayani (2023) . Furthermore, with the emergence of deep learning, quadrupeds are becoming progressively more autonomous: their gaits are increasingly adaptable, and they can perform intelligent real-time monitoring and decision-making based on sensor data Wang et al. (2024) . Thus, to enable quadruped deployment at scale, novel fields of applications with well defined tasks and challenges should be investigated. Table 1: Potential applications for quadruped robots in roof environments. Category Tasks Manipulation Refurbishment and re-roofing Health and Safety Executive (2020) Maintenance and cleaning Health and Safety Executive (2020) Painting and protection Highspecroofing (2024) Stripping and dismantling of roofs Health and Safety Executive (2020) Cutting overhanging vegetation Highspecroofing (2024) Snow removal Highspecroofing (2024) Precision Installation of ancillary equipment Health and Safety Executive (2020) Chimney sweep Transport Roof materials Health and Safety Executive (2020) Plant watering Information Inspection and surveying Health and Safety Executive (2020) A potential new environment for quadruped robots to operate in is presented by roofs, offering a unique set of challenges and tasks. Quadrupeds could be deployed in roof environments for a multitude of applications, which are presented in Table 1 . Residential buildings often feature moderate to steep inclines ( 25 ° to 60 ° 25\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}60\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} ), smooth roof tile surfaces, and regularly repeating structural elements such as convex and flat areas or tile row steps, making locomotion inherently difficult Blaß () . Conversely, the repetitive nature of standardized roof tiles provides an opportunity to tailor quadrupeds feet specifically for this environment. This work provides: • The first systematic experimental evaluation of quadruped locomotion in tiled roof environments. • Quantitative failure thresholds for balanced standing, get-up/lie-down motions, and incline walking establishing a baseline for future research. • A motion-capture-based methodology for objectively observing foot slippage during inclined locomotion. 2 Evaluating Quadruped Locomotion in Roof Environments In roof environments, quadruped locomotion performance is primarily determined by two factors: friction and stability. To objectively evaluate and compare quadruped locomotion, an accurate measurement methodology is required. In this work the main focus is placed on friction as the primary performance indicator, while loss of stability, referred to as critical failure, marks the upper performance limit when the robot falls. Friction can be estimated by measuring slippage on a defined incline angle. This necessitates an external measurement system. For this purpose, the OptiTrack system – a motion capture system based on infrared light and reflective markers – is employed. The system can be calibrated to achieve a measurement accuracy of below 1.0 mm 1.0\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} OptiTrack () . The feet of a quadruped robot are the primary, and often only, components that directly interact with the environment Li et al. (2023) . While other end-effectors in robotics, such as hands and grippers, have received considerable attention, the development of non-humanoid feet has received less focus Catalano et al. (2022) ; Eckert and Ijspeert (2016) . Currently, most major manufacturers and research institutes employ a simple round foot geometry Ranjan et al. (2024) ; Kalogroulis et al. (2024) . This design is widely adopted due to its simplicity, robustness, and reliable performance across diverse environments Kalogroulis et al. (2024) . Further, the ball-shaped design allows for a simplified contact modeling approach, reducing the simulated contact to a point or line Eckert and Ijspeert (2016) . However, such feet provide a limited contact area, resulting in high stress concentrations and an increased risk of slippage, particularly on inclined surfaces, as rubber friction is area dependent Ranjan et al. (2024) ; Kalogroulis et al. (2024) ; Richhariya et al. (2023) . Moreover, ball feet lack adaptability to varying terrains, restricting their effectiveness in complex environments Ranjan et al. (2024) . Due to these drawbacks and the highly difficult roof environment, the development of customized and environment adapted feet is worth investigating in future work. 3 Experimental Setup As a preliminary experiment the dynamic coefficient of friction f f of the ball feet was measured by using the internal force-torque sensor of a UR10e . The foot is pushed onto the roof tile surface with a defined normal force of 60 N, which is approximately the average force applied to a single foot of the Go2 during walking. Next, the foot is dragged over the tile for a distance of 100 mm 100\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} , while the antagonistic friction force is measured. The experiment is repeated 10 times, both on flat and curved sections of the roof tile. The mean coefficient of friction is calculated through the ratio between measured tangential force F T F_{T} and applied normal force F N F_{N} depicted in Eq. 1 . The dynamic coefficient was measured instead of the static coefficient, because due to the nature of the soft and hollow rubber feet of the Go2 , a static coefficient could not reliably be measured, as pre-slip tangential force were affected by progressive foot deformation. f = F T F N = t ​ a ​ n ​ ( ρ ) \displaystyle f=\frac{F_{T}}{F_{N}}=tan(\rho) (1) To objectively assess the performance of the Go2 (software version 1.4.4) and create a baseline for future comparison with custom feet, an adjustable test rig of a roof environment was developed (see Fig. 1 ). As surface material the Frankfurther Pfanne was chosen, which is the most common type of roof tile in Germany BMI Deutschland GmbH () . With the Go2 , three core skills were examined: balancing on continuously increasing inclines, get-up/lie-down sequences, and incline walking. To create statistical significance every experiment is repeated ten times. For balancing, the robot was placed facing uphill on a 0 ° 0\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} incline, which was gradually increased until balance was lost, revealing failure modes under static conditions. Get-up and lie-down performance was assessed on progressively steeper inclines in three orientations (uphill, downhill, sideways), with success defined as completing both actions in each configuration. article.body:
Unitree Go2 roof tests expose limits on 25° slopes

A commercial Unitree Go2 quadruped was tested for locomotion on a dedicated roof-surface rig, not during construction work on a live roof. With its standard ball feet, the robot slipped more as the incline increased; the paper reports that slippage rose quadratically with slope angle. Getting up and lying down worked only on small inclines, while critical failures occurred regularly at 25°.

The paper does not disclose a training method or specify the robot’s autonomy level. It establishes a baseline for physical testing of roof locomotion, not reliable operation on roofs or capability to carry out construction tasks.
